description: Polaris Scholar is an interdisciplinary team of innovators, researchers, and problem-solvers participating in the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Inspired by the North Star a timeless symbol of guidance and navigation our team combines data science, space exploration, and academic curiosity to transform complex NASA open data into accessible, real-world solutions.
summary: Project Aegis is an interactive space mission design game that allows players to experience the challenges of real-world space exploration. Players can design spacecraft, configure scientific instruments, build rockets, plan launches, and complete missions across Earth, the Sun, the Moon, and Mars. The game addresses the NASA Space Mission Design Game challenge by transforming complex aerospace engineering concepts into an engaging, hands-on learning experience. It features five missions inspired by real NASA space programs and integrates NASA's EONET API to retrieve live natural-event data for dynamic Earth-observation scenarios. Through interactive simulations and 3D visualizations, players learn about rocket propulsion, orbital mechanics, satellite technology, and planetary exploration while developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Project Aegis is important because it makes space science more accessible, encourages interest in STEM education, and demonstrates how NASA data and space technology can help us understand challenges on Earth and explore beyond it.
details:
1. What does your project do or how does it work?

Project Aegis is an interactive space exploration game that allows players to experience what it takes to design and operate space missions. Players can build spacecraft, select scientific instruments, construct rockets, plan launches, and complete missions involving Earth, the Sun, the Moon, and Mars. The game features five progressive missions inspired by real NASA space missions. It also uses NASA's EONET API to retrieve live natural-event information and generate dynamic Earth-observation challenges.

2. What benefits does your project have?

Project Aegis makes complex space science and engineering concepts easier to understand through interactive gameplay. Players can learn about rocket engineering, orbital mechanics, satellite technology, remote sensing, and planetary science. It also encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and decision-making by challenging players to overcome engineering obstacles and complete scientific objectives.

3. What is the intended impact of your project?

The project aims to make space science more accessible and enjoyable, especially for students and young people. It seeks to inspire the next generation to explore STEM fields, particularly aerospace engineering and astronomy. It also demonstrates how NASA data and space technology can help us understand environmental challenges and protect our planet.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Project Aegis was developed as a browser-based application using HTML5, CSS, and JavaScript, with React for the user interface, Tailwind CSS for styling, and Three.js for interactive 3D graphics. Google AI Studio was also used as an AI-powered development and prototyping tool to help build the application. The project integrates NASA's EONET API to retrieve natural-event information and uses Google Fonts for typography. No specialized physical hardware was required.

5. How is your project creative?

Project Aegis combines spacecraft design, rocket construction, launch simulations, and scientific exploration into one connected gaming experience. Instead of simply reading about space missions, players actively make engineering decisions and experience the consequences of their choices. The game also connects fictional missions with real NASA missions and incorporates live Earth-observation data to make some challenges more dynamic and relevant to real-world events.

6. What factors did your team consider?

During development, the team considered scientific accuracy, engineering feasibility, educational value, accessibility, and user experience. The game incorporates engineering constraints such as spacecraft mass, power consumption, propulsion, and communication capacity. The team also considered performance, progressive difficulty, and the reliability of live NASA data. When live data is unavailable or insufficient, the game provides predefined scenarios to ensure that players can continue their missions.
